REINS: A Self-Evolving Agent Harness for Real-Time Trajectory Planning

Zhihong Cui    Hengyu Liu    Haoran Tang Affiliation: Department of Computing, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong SAR, China    Shijun Liu Affiliation: Shandong Key Laboratory of Foundational Software, School of Software, Shandong University, China    Amir Taherkordi Affiliation: Department of Informatics, University of Oslo, Norway    Tor Skeie Affiliation: Department of Informatics, University of Oslo, Norway Affiliation: Simula Research Laboratory, Norway Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Aalborg University, Denmark
Abstract

Agent harnesses—runtime scaffolds that wrap an LLM’s reasoning loop with tool dispatch, verification, and persistent memory—have become the standard substrate for deploying LLMs as autonomous agents, as demonstrated by Claude Code and Codex in software engineering. In trajectory planning, however, this paradigm has not taken hold: existing LLM-based trajectory planning methods either keep the LLM in the decision loop, exceeding the millisecond-level control budget, or offload it to offline rules or training-time supervision—leaving the runtime planner non-evolving. Intermediate hybrids still lack the verification-and-consolidation loop that makes harnesses reliable. We ask: what runtime harness would let an LLM planner meet real-time constraints while self-evolving into a deployable one? We propose REINS, a harness built on three LLM–planner couplings: LLM outputs are (i) grounded to a learned variable-level dynamics model, (ii) verified via calibrated predicates and forward rollout, and (iii) consolidated into an indexed rule memory that serves future scenes in 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log n) without re-invoking the LLM. The harness closes a self-evolution loop: familiar scenes resolve by memory lookup; novel scenes invoke the LLM, whose verified outputs enrich the memory. Without modifying LLM weights, REINS attains 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9–4.6 ms latency on simulated and real-world benchmarks at the tactical decision layer, with LLM invocation rate monotonically declining as memory matures. Code: https://github.com/ZhihongCui/REINS.

1 Introduction

Trajectory planning is the safety-critical core of autonomous driving: each decision must respect traffic rules, anticipate other agents, and complete within a millisecond-level control budget (e.g., 50 ms at 20 Hz) (Zhang et al., 2021a; Falcone et al., 2007; Lenz et al., 2016; Li et al., 2024b; Montgomery, 1983). Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) bring rich semantic priors over traffic norms, agent intent, and safety reasoning that classical planners lack (Manas et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2024; Mao et al., 2024; Sha et al., 2023; Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a), yet integrating their reasoning into the runtime loop is bottlenecked: each LLM query takes seconds—orders of magnitude over the control budget—and naive integration leaves the planner either too slow to act or unable to adapt as deployment proceeds.

This is precisely the kind of deployment problem—running a stochastic LLM inside a low-latency, safety-sensitive loop—that the agent harness paradigm has recently addressed in software engineering. An agent harness wraps the LLM with a thin runtime layer of tool dispatch, intermediate-result verification, persistent memory, and safety enforcement—as exemplified by systems like Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor-Agent. On Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026), harness design has emerged as a primary driver of ranking, with automatic harness optimization surpassing hand-engineered baselines (Lee et al., 2026). Trajectory planning, however, is a sharp test of the paradigm: its millisecond-level control budget is much tighter than the seconds-to-minutes scale at which coding harnesses operate, and the safety stakes are higher. In this regime, the harness’s generic functions specialize into three couplings between LLM and planner, illustrated in Figure 1: when an LLM suggests “keep a safe distance” in a car-following scene, the runtime must (i) ground the suggestion to physical state variables (TTC, THW, DHW), (ii) verify the resulting maneuver via forward rollout over a multi-step horizon, and (iii) consolidate the verified maneuver into an indexed rule memory.

Existing LLM-based trajectory planning methods span two extremes plus intermediate hybrids, none of which constitutes a harness in the above sense: runtime invocation methods keep the LLM in the decision loop but exceed the millisecond-level budget by orders of magnitude (Fu et al., 2024; Mao et al., 2024; Sha et al., 2023); offline extraction methods discard the LLM at runtime and freeze the planner against scenarios the offline corpus did not anticipate (Li et al., 2024a; Tang et al., 2025); and hybrid designs partially orchestrate the LLM at runtime but stop short of a full harness, lacking explicit verification of LLM commitments and consolidation of verified ones into reusable structure (Cui et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025). Across all three, the LLM’s reasoning is either too slow to act on or too detached from the loop to evolve with deployment.

This raises our central question: what runtime harness would let an LLM planner satisfy real-time constraints while self-evolving into a deployable one? Each of the three couplings is non-trivial under real-time control: grounding requires bridging natural-language commitments to the planner’s threshold semantics (Wang et al., 2025; Zhai et al., 2025); verification must catch stochastic, occasionally unsafe LLM outputs before they reach control (Manas et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2025); and consolidation must escape per-call LLM latency (Fu et al., 2024; Mao et al., 2024) via a memory pattern emerging in agentic AI (Wang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024) but not yet transferred to real-time planning. The three are also jointly necessary: without grounding, verification has nothing to check; without verification, consolidation stores unverified content; without consolidation, every scene re-pays the LLM latency cost. When all three are addressed, a self-evolution loop emerges: familiar scenes resolve from the consolidated memory in 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log n) time, novel scenes invoke the LLM, whose verified outputs enrich the memory, and reliance on the LLM decreases monotonically as memory matures, with no LLM weight update.

We propose REINS, a concrete realization of this harness pattern, instantiated for trajectory planning in driving, that addresses each coupling as follows. Grounding. We learn a world dynamics model over a factored variable space, fusing LLM-derived semantic priors with data-driven dependency discovery. Group-weighted ridge regression selects each variable’s parents, and a per-variable Transformer predicts its evolution under the discovered graph. Every LLM output can then be projected onto this variable space and rolled out under the learned dynamics. Verification. We compile each LLM-proposed maneuver into calibrated predicates with thresholds derived from data (z-score, quantile, or absolute). Predicates are evaluated against the rollout produced by the dynamics model, and only commitments whose predicted trajectory satisfies all guards are released to control. Hallucinated or unsafe commitments are filtered before any maneuver is issued. Consolidation. We persist verified commitments in an indexed rule memory backed by a graph database, keyed by the grounding variables that triggered them. At runtime, parameterized graph queries retrieve scene-relevant rules in 𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\mathcal{O}(\log n) time without any LLM call. Recurring scenes are thus served by memory lookup, and the LLM is invoked only on a miss. Together, the three close the self-evolution loop: at each scene the planner first consults the memory; on a miss the LLM is invoked, its output grounded against the dynamics model, verified by rollout, and—if it passes—committed to memory for the next encounter. We provide an empirical demonstration that, under such a harness, an LLM planner monotonically reduces its own LLM-call rate while preserving safety and compliance. Our contributions can be summarized as:

  • •

    We extend the agent-harness paradigm to real-time trajectory planning, identifying three couplings—grounding, verification, consolidation—any such harness must enforce, and instantiate it for driving; only the variable schema and the action space are domain-specific (Appendix D.1).

  • •

    We design REINS, a harness that instantiates the three couplings via a learned world dynamics model, calibrated predicates with rollout verification, and an indexed rule memory.

  • •

    We provide the first empirical evidence of self-evolution in real-time LLM trajectory planning: LLM invocation rate decreases monotonically over deployment with no LLM weight update.

  • •

    We evaluate REINS on simulated and real-world driving benchmarks at the tactical decision layer, achieving 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9–4.6 ms planning latency—well within the real-time control budget.

2 Related Work

LLM-Based Trajectory Planning. Recent LLM-based trajectory planners fall along three lines, each realizing some couplings while leaving others open. Runtime invocation methods keep the LLM in the decision loop. DiLu (Fu et al., 2024) pairs LLM reasoning with an experience-replay memory; Agent-Driver (Mao et al., 2024) treats the LLM as an orchestrator over perception and planning tools; LanguageMPC (Sha et al., 2023) feeds chain-of-thought outputs into MPC. These systems gain semantic flexibility, but each LLM query takes seconds, and any output that reaches the planner is implicitly trusted, lacking the calibrated checks proposed for stochastic LLM outputs in safety-critical settings (Manas et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2025).

Offline extraction methods sit at the opposite end. LLaDA (Li et al., 2024a) extracts location-specific rules from driver handbooks, DriReg (Cai et al., 2024) retrieves regulatory text via RAG, and Plan-R1 (Tang et al., 2025) distills LLM-shaped rewards into a reinforcement-learning policy. Removing the LLM at runtime buys real-time inference, but the planner becomes static, unable to consolidate new commitments against learned driving dynamics (Wang et al., 2025; Zhai et al., 2025) or to adapt to scenarios the offline corpus did not anticipate.

Hybrid designs partially orchestrate the LLM at runtime. C-TRAIL (Cui et al., 2026) runs a closed-loop Recall–Plan–Update cycle with trust-weighted MCTS injection; LeAD (Zhang et al., 2025) pairs an end-to-end planner with a redundant LLM reasoning track. These improve over either extreme but lack explicit verification of LLM commitments and consolidation of verified ones into reusable structure; none grounds, verifies, and consolidates LLM outputs jointly under a real-time harness.

Agent Harnesses for LLM Deployment. Outside trajectory planning, the deployment of LLMs into real-world tasks has converged on the agent harness pattern: a thin runtime layer that wraps the LLM with tool dispatch, intermediate-result verification, persistent memory, and safety enforcement. In autonomous coding, systems such as Claude Code and Codex turn general-purpose LLMs into reliable software engineers, and harness design has become a primary driver of ranking on Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). In open-ended decision-making, Voyager (Wang et al., 2023) accumulates a skill library of executable code through curiosity-driven exploration; Eureka (Ma et al., 2024) iteratively refines reward functions by evolutionary search over LLM proposals; ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024) distills task-specific experience into a retrievable knowledge base. These harnesses share three structural elements with REINS—grounding into a domain primitive space, verification of LLM outputs, and persistent reuse of verified ones—but none operate under millisecond real-time budgets nor expose their LLMs to the safety-critical constraints.

3 Preliminaries

We formalize the harness’s primitives: a factored variable space (Section 3.1); a world dynamics model for grounding (Section 3.2); an executable rule representation for verification and consolidation (Section 3.3); and the problem definition (Section 3.4). Full variable lists, template specifications, and the macro-group dependency enumeration appear in Appendix A.

3.1 Driving Environment

Definition 3.1 (Factored Variable Structure).

A factored variable structure is (𝒳,ℋ,ℰ𝒢,ℰℋ)(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{H},\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{G}},\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}}): 𝒳={X1,…,Xd}\mathcal{X}=\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{d}\} are observable variables (e.g., TTC, THW, DHW, ego_speed, lead_speed, road_friction); ℋ={Env,Traffic,Ego,Action,Outcome}\mathcal{H}=\{\textsc{Env},\textsc{Traffic},\textsc{Ego},\textsc{Action},\textsc{Outcome}\} groups them by semantic role (Chen et al., 2025); ℰ𝒢⊆𝒳×ℋ\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{G}}\subseteq\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{H} assigns each variable to a group; and ℰℋ⊆ℋ×ℋ\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}}\subseteq\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{H} specifies permissible group-level dependencies (Eq. 10 in Appendix A.1).

Definition 3.2 (State and Action Spaces).

The state st∈𝒮=∏idom⁡(Xi)s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}=\prod_{i}\mathrm{dom}(X_{i}) is a complete variable assignment. The action space 𝒜={LANE_LEFT,LANE_RIGHT,FASTER,SLOWER,IDLE}\mathcal{A}=\{\texttt{LANE\_LEFT},\texttt{LANE\_RIGHT},\texttt{FASTER},\texttt{SLOWER},\texttt{IDLE}\} is a finite set of discrete meta-actions for the ego vehicle.

The meta-actions are the interface of the tactical (behavior-planning) layer in the standard stack decomposition (Paden et al., 2016); continuous low-level controllers execute them, and all safety reasoning below (TTC, headway, accelerations) remains continuous.

3.2 World Dynamics Model

Definition 3.3 (Dependency Graph and Dynamics).

A dependency graph is a weighted DAG 𝒢=(𝒳,ℰ,w)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{E},w) with w:ℰ→ℝw:\mathcal{E}\to\mathbb{R}, where edges (Xi,Xj)∈ℰ(X_{i},X_{j})\in\mathcal{E} are admissible only if (h⁡(Xi),h⁡(Xj))∈ℰℋ(h(X_{i}),h(X_{j}))\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}} (Giamattei et al., 2024). A dynamics function set ℱ={fi}i=1d\mathcal{F}=\{f_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d} predicts each variable from its parents over a temporal lag LL (Peters et al., 2017):

X^it+1=fi(Pa(Xi)t−L+1:t),Pa(Xi)={Xj∣(Xj,Xi)∈ℰ}.\hat{X}_{i}^{t+1}=f_{i}\big(\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i})^{t-L+1:t}\big),\quad\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i})=\{X_{j}\mid(X_{j},X_{i})\in\mathcal{E}\}. (1)

An HH-step rollout from sts_{t} under (at,…,at+H−1)(a_{t},\ldots,a_{t+H-1}) yields ξ^=(s^t+1,…,s^t+H)\hat{\xi}=(\hat{s}_{t+1},\ldots,\hat{s}_{t+H}).

3.3 Rule Representation

Definition 3.4 (Predicate).

A predicate is a Boolean function p(s)=𝕀[s[Xi]≺τ]p(s)=\mathbb{I}[s[X_{i}]\prec\tau] with comparison operator ≺∈{<,>,≤,≥}\prec\in\{<,>,\leq,\geq\} and threshold τ∈ℝ\tau\in\mathbb{R}.

TTC and THW guards are the surrogate safety measures of traffic engineering (Gettman and Head, 2003); their calibrated thresholds act as RSS-style safe-distance bounds (Shalev-Shwartz et al., 2017).

Definition 3.5 (Rule Template).

A rule template TT specifies how predicates compose (Manas et al., 2024). We use seven templates: IF-THEN, AND-THEN, THRESHOLD, PRIORITY, MULTI-ACTION, WEIGHTED-ACTION, and TEMPORAL-CHAIN (specifications and examples in Appendix A.2).

Definition 3.6 (Executable Rule).

An executable rule is a tuple r=(T,𝒫r,ar,cr)r=(T,\mathcal{P}_{r},a_{r},c_{r}) with template TT, guard predicates 𝒫r\mathcal{P}_{r}, recommended action ar∈𝒜a_{r}\in\mathcal{A}, and confidence cr∈[0,1]c_{r}\in[0,1]. Activation requires all guards to hold:

Exec⁡(r,st)=⋀p∈𝒫rp⁡(st).\mathrm{Exec}(r,s_{t})=\bigwedge_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{r}}p(s_{t}). (2)

3.4 Problem Definition

Definition 3.7 (Self-Evolving Agent Harness for Trajectory Planning).

Let 𝒟={(st,at,st+1)}\mathcal{D}=\{(s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1})\} be a driving dataset and ℳ\mathcal{M} a pre-trained LLM. The harness problem is to construct ⟨𝒢^,ℱ^,ℛ,π⟩\langle\hat{\mathcal{G}},\hat{\mathcal{F}},\mathcal{R},\pi\rangle where 𝒢^,ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{G}},\hat{\mathcal{F}} are learned from 𝒟\mathcal{D} with priors from ℳ\mathcal{M} (Def. 3.3), ℛ\mathcal{R} is an indexed rule memory compiled offline from ℳ\mathcal{M} (Def. 3.6), and π:𝒮→𝒜\pi:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{A} is a policy that, at each sts_{t}, retrieves ℛt=Retrieve⁡(st,ℛ)⊆ℛ\mathcal{R}_{t}=\mathrm{Retrieve}(s_{t},\mathcal{R})\subseteq\mathcal{R} and proceeds as follows:

  • •

    (hit) if ℛt≠∅\mathcal{R}_{t}\neq\emptyset, π\pi scores actions over ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} and verifies them by rollout under ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} within a real-time budget;

  • •

    (miss) otherwise, ℳ\mathcal{M} proposes a candidate commitment, which is grounded via (𝒢^,ℱ^)(\hat{\mathcal{G}},\hat{\mathcal{F}}) and verified by rollout; if all predicates pass, the commitment is compiled into a rule rr and ℛ←ℛ∪{r}\mathcal{R}\leftarrow\mathcal{R}\cup\{r\}.

The parameters of ℳ\mathcal{M} remain unchanged, and ℛ\mathcal{R} is monotone non-decreasing; under stationarity of the scene distribution, the per-scene LLM invocation rate Pr[ℛt=∅]\Pr[\mathcal{R}_{t}=\emptyset] is non-increasing.

4 Methodology

REINS realizes the harness as a two-phase system (Figure 2). Offline Preparation (Section 4.1) prepares the world dynamics 𝒢^,ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{G}},\hat{\mathcal{F}} for grounding and an initial rule memory ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} for offline consolidation. Online Runtime (Section 4.2) executes a per-scene loop: rule-guided planning performs retrieval, scoring, and verification over ℛ\mathcal{R}, and online rule acquisition handles memory misses by querying ℳ\mathcal{M} and writing verified rules back to ℛ\mathcal{R}, closing the self-evolution loop.

4.1 Offline Preparation

4.1.1 World Dynamics Learning

This module realizes grounding: we jointly learn dependency graph 𝒢^\hat{\mathcal{G}} and dynamics functions ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} by combining LLM semantic priors with data-driven structure discovery. The full derivation and the dynamics loss are in Appendix A.4.1.

Dependency Graph. The LLM provides edge confidence πi​j∈[0,1]\pi_{ij}\in[0,1] for each candidate edge Xj→XiX_{j}\to X_{i} (Appendix A.5); combined with macro-group constraints (Eq. 10), the unified prior is π~i​j=απi​j+(1−α)𝕀{(h(Xj),h(Xi))∈ℰℋ}\tilde{\pi}_{ij}=\alpha\,\pi_{ij}+(1-\alpha)\,\mathbb{I}\{(h(X_{j}),h(X_{i}))\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}}\}. For each XiX_{i}, prior-guided ridge regression (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970) predicts its value from lagged neighbors with adaptive penalty λi​j=λ0​(1−π~i​j)ρ\lambda_{ij}=\lambda_{0}(1-\tilde{\pi}_{ij})^{\rho}, so high-prior edges are weakly regularized:

𝐰^i=arg⁡min⁡∑t=LN𝐰⁡(Xit−∑j≠i,ℓwj​ℓ​Xjt−ℓ)2+∑j≠iλi​j​‖𝐰j‖22.\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{w}}\sum_{t=L}^{N}\Big(X_{i}^{t}-\textstyle\sum_{j\neq i,\ell}w_{j\ell}X_{j}^{t-\ell}\Big)^{2}+\sum_{j\neq i}\lambda_{ij}\|\mathbf{w}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}. (3)

Pa⁡(Xi)\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i}) retains the top-KK variables by ∑ℓ|w^j​ℓ|\sum_{\ell}|\hat{w}_{j\ell}|, yielding ℰ^\hat{\mathcal{E}} and weights w^​(Xj,Xi)=∑ℓ|w^j​ℓ|\hat{w}(X_{j},X_{i})=\sum_{\ell}|\hat{w}_{j\ell}|.

Dynamics Functions. Given 𝒢^\hat{\mathcal{G}}, each fif_{i} is a multi-head Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) trained to predict Xit+1X_{i}^{t+1} from Pa(Xi)t−L+1:t\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i})^{t-L+1:t} via mean squared error (loss form in Eq. 14). Training curves and hyperparameters are in Appendix C.1.

4.1.2 Rule Compilation

This module realizes offline consolidation: compiling LLM knowledge into executable rules. Full equations and per-step prose are in Appendix A.4.2.

Rule Structure Generation. For each edge (Xj,Xi)∈ℰ^(X_{j},X_{i})\in\hat{\mathcal{E}}, the LLM generates a rule r=(T,𝒫r,ar,cr)r=(T,\mathcal{P}_{r},a_{r},c_{r}) (Eq. 15) with template TT (Def. 3.5), guard predicates 𝒫r\mathcal{P}_{r} with symbolic thresholds, recommended action ar∈𝒜a_{r}\in\mathcal{A}, and confidence crc_{r} derived from edge weight w^​(Xj,Xi)\hat{w}(X_{j},X_{i}) (prompts in Appendix A.5).

Threshold Calibration. Each predicate’s threshold τi\tau_{i} is calibrated from 𝒟\mathcal{D} in three forms (Luo et al., 2024)—z-score μi+ζ​σi\mu_{i}+\zeta\sigma_{i}, quantile Qi​(ζ)Q_{i}(\zeta), or absolute constant τ0\tau_{0}—and the comparison operator ≺\prec is selected to maximize separability of safety outcome y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\}:

≺∗=argmax≺∈{<,>}|𝔼[y∣Xi≺τi]−𝔼[y∣Xi⊀τi]|.\prec^{*}=\arg\max_{\prec\in\{<,>\}}\big|\mathbb{E}[y\mid X_{i}\prec\tau_{i}]-\mathbb{E}[y\mid X_{i}\not\prec\tau_{i}]\big|. (4)

Rule activation then follows Eq. 2.

Graph Database Storage. Compiled rules are stored in a Neo4j graph database (Webber, 2012) with rule nodes connected to variable nodes via TRIGGERS (input) and AFFECTS (output) edges, enabling O⁡(log⁡|ℛ|)O(\log|\mathcal{R}|) retrieval. The full schema (Figure 3) is in Appendix A.4.2; database statistics are in Appendix C.7.1.

4.2 Online Runtime

4.2.1 Rule-Guided Planning

This module realizes the runtime planning loop of Def. 3.7—retrieval, scoring, and verification (details in Appendix A.4.3).

Scene-Aware Retrieval. Given sts_{t}, active variables {Xi}\{X_{i}\} trigger parameterized Cypher queries (Francis et al., 2018) generated by the LLM (read-only, schema-constrained; Appendix A.5). The retrieval map G:({Xi},K)↦ℛt⊆ℛG:(\{X_{i}\},K)\mapsto\mathcal{R}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{R} (Eq. 17) returns up to KK rules ranked by confidence, restricted to triggers whose dependency direction respects the macro-group constraints.

Action Scoring. For each r∈ℛtr\in\mathcal{R}_{t} activated via Eq. 2, a Transformer-based scorer (Liang et al., 2022) produces relevance Srel​(r,st)∈[0,1]S_{\text{rel}}(r,s_{t})\in[0,1] and action preference Sact​(r,st,a)S_{\text{act}}(r,s_{t},a), yielding combined score f⁡(r,a∣st)=Srel⋅Sact⋅crf(r,a\mid s_{t})=S_{\text{rel}}\cdot S_{\text{act}}\cdot c_{r} (Eqs. 18–19; training loss in Eq. 20). Multiple rules recommending action aa, denoted ℛt​(a)={r∈ℛt∣ar=a}\mathcal{R}_{t}(a)=\{r\in\mathcal{R}_{t}\mid a_{r}=a\}, are aggregated by noisy-OR:

P⁡(a∣st)∝ 1−∏r∈ℛt​(a)(1−f⁡(r,a∣st)).P(a\mid s_{t})\;\propto\;1-\prod_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{t}(a)}\big(1-f(r,a\mid s_{t})\big). (5)

The full normalized form and argmax decoder are in Appendix A.4.3.

Trajectory Verification. The learned dynamics ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} verifies safety via forward rollout. For the top-MM actions ranked by P⁡(a∣st)P(a\mid s_{t}), we predict HH-step trajectories ξ^​(a)=(s^t+1,…,s^t+H)\hat{\xi}(a)=(\hat{s}_{t+1},\ldots,\hat{s}_{t+H}) via s^t+h+1=Φ⁡(s^t+h,a,𝒢^,ℱ^)\hat{s}_{t+h+1}=\Phi(\hat{s}_{t+h},a;\hat{\mathcal{G}},\hat{\mathcal{F}}) (Eq. 22), and select at⋆=arg⁡maxa∈𝒜M⁡J⁡(ξ^​(a))a^{\star}_{t}=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{M}}J(\hat{\xi}(a)), where JJ penalizes collisions, rule violations, and control effort (Appendix B.2); the first control is executed in receding-horizon (Zhang et al., 2021b).

4.2.2 Online Rule Acquisition

This module realizes Def. 3.7’s miss-handling path through four steps (full equations and the monotonicity argument in Appendix A.4.4).

Miss Detection. We operationalize the miss criterion (ℛt=∅\mathcal{R}_{t}=\emptyset) with an additional confidence guard against weakly supported matches:

Miss(st)=𝕀[ℛt=∅]∨𝕀[maxr∈ℛt,a∈𝒜f(r,a∣st)<η],\mathrm{Miss}(s_{t})\;=\;\mathbb{I}\!\left[\mathcal{R}_{t}=\emptyset\right]\;\vee\;\mathbb{I}\!\left[\max_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{t},\,a\in\mathcal{A}}f(r,a\mid s_{t})<\eta\right], (6)

with tuned threshold η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1).

Rule Proposal and Online Verification. On a miss, ℳ\mathcal{M} proposes r~=(T~,𝒫~,a~,c~)\tilde{r}=(\tilde{T},\tilde{\mathcal{P}},\tilde{a},\tilde{c}) (Eq. 23) conforming to Defs. 3.4–3.5 (Appendix A.5). Symbolic thresholds in 𝒫~\tilde{\mathcal{P}} are calibrated on a sliding window 𝒟tW={st−W+1,…,st}\mathcal{D}_{t}^{W}=\{s_{t-W+1},\ldots,s_{t}\} so they track the current distribution. The harness then rolls out a~\tilde{a} from sts_{t} under ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} and accepts r~\tilde{r} iff every predicate holds along the rollout:

Accept⁡(r~,st)=⋀p∈𝒫~⋀h=1Hp⁡(s^t+h).\mathrm{Accept}(\tilde{r},s_{t})\;=\;\bigwedge_{p\in\tilde{\mathcal{P}}}\bigwedge_{h=1}^{H}p(\hat{s}_{t+h}). (7)

On rejection the planner falls back to arg⁡maxa⁡P⁡(a∣st)\arg\max_{a}P(a\mid s_{t}) over ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} if ℛt≠∅\mathcal{R}_{t}\neq\emptyset; otherwise the harness raises a human-takeover alert and executes the safest action under ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} by maximizing minimum lookahead TTC (Eq. 24 in Appendix A.4.4).

Memory Update. Accepted r~\tilde{r} is keyed by content hash κ⁡(r~):=κ⁡(T~,𝒫~,a~)\kappa(\tilde{r}):=\kappa(\tilde{T},\tilde{\mathcal{P}},\tilde{a}) and inserted into Neo4j; on collision, confidences are averaged instead of duplicating the node:

ℛ⟵{ℛ∪{r~}κ⁡(r~)∉Keys⁡(ℛ),ℛ​ with ​cr′←12​(cr′+c~)∃r′∈ℛ:κ⁡(r′)=κ⁡(r~).\mathcal{R}\;\longleftarrow\;\begin{cases}\mathcal{R}\cup\{\tilde{r}\}&\kappa(\tilde{r})\notin\mathrm{Keys}(\mathcal{R}),\\[2.0pt] \mathcal{R}\text{ with }c_{r^{\prime}}\leftarrow\tfrac{1}{2}(c_{r^{\prime}}+\tilde{c})&\exists\,r^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R}:\kappa(r^{\prime})=\kappa(\tilde{r}).\end{cases} (8)

The collision-branch rationale (averaging vs. duplication, exclusion of c~\tilde{c} from κ\kappa) is in Appendix A.4.4.

Self-Evolution Properties. Eq. 8 structurally enforces |ℛt+1|≥|ℛt||\mathcal{R}_{t+1}|\geq|\mathcal{R}_{t}| (memory monotonicity) and θℳ≡θℳ(0)\theta_{\mathcal{M}}\equiv\theta_{\mathcal{M}}^{(0)} (no LLM update). Under stationarity of the scene distribution, the per-state miss rate is non-increasing as ℛ\mathcal{R} accumulates coverage:

|ℛt+1|≥|ℛt|,Pr⁡[Miss⁡(st+1)]≤Pr⁡[Miss⁡(st)],θℳ≡θℳ(0),|\mathcal{R}_{t+1}|\geq|\mathcal{R}_{t}|,\quad\Pr[\mathrm{Miss}(s_{t+1})]\leq\Pr[\mathrm{Miss}(s_{t})],\quad\theta_{\mathcal{M}}\equiv\theta_{\mathcal{M}}^{(0)}, (9)

so the per-scene LLM invocation rate decays monotonically with Pr⁡[Miss]\Pr[\mathrm{Miss}] (full argument in Appendix A.4.4; validated in Section 5.4).

5 Experiment

The main body reports overall comparison (Section 5.2), ablation (Section 5.3), self-evolution dynamics on Highway (Section 5.4), and a summary of the robustness, transfer, and scalability results. Appendices C and D report trajectory accuracy, sensitivity, extended self-evolution traces, a case study, the rule database, and the fairness and robustness studies.

5.1 Experiment Setting

Datasets and Protocols. We evaluate REINS on four highway-env (Leurent, 2018) scenarios—Highway, Merge, Roundabout, Intersection (100 steps at 5 Hz, 15 observable vehicles per episode)—and two drone-captured real-world datasets (Krajewski et al., 2018; Krajewski et al., 2020): highD (German highway, 4,237 vehicles, 578 lane changes) and rounD (German roundabouts, 2,156 vehicles, 423 yield/merge events). Surrounding vehicles in simulation are reactive (IDM car-following (Treiber et al., 2000) with MOBIL lane changes (Kesting et al., 2007)), so they brake, yield, and change lanes in response to the ego. The real-world datasets run in closed-loop replay: one recorded vehicle is controlled by the planner while the others follow their recorded trajectories, so these rows reflect human behavior rather than a simulator’s; a collision is registered when bounding boxes overlap or the ego leaves the drivable lane. A reactive-replay variant following the nuPlan protocol (Caesar et al., 2021) is in Appendix D.6. All methods observe clean factored variables; perception, tracking, and map errors lie outside the evaluated layer (Section 6).

Evaluation Metrics. Compl. (Rule Compliance) is the fraction of steps at which all active rules hold, measured for each method against its own executable rule set; an audit of all methods against REINS’s compiled set as a common reference leaves the ordering unchanged (Appendix D.2). RE (Risk-aware Efficiency) is task reward minus a TTC-based risk penalty. CR (Collision Rate) is the fraction of episodes with at least one contact among the 15 vehicles over 100 steps, an episode-level rate in deliberately stressed traffic. PE (Planning Efficiency) is the mean wall-clock ms of the synchronous action-selection computation per step for every method; for REINS it excludes the asynchronous rule-acquisition pipeline, profiled separately in Appendix D.8. TTC and THW, which underlie the guards and the RE penalty, are the surrogate safety measures of traffic engineering (Gettman and Head, 2003), and Compl. and CR echo the rule-conformance and collision outcomes reported in scenario-based safety assessment (Riedmaier et al., 2020). Results are averaged over five seeds; formal definitions in Appendix B.2.

Baselines. We compare with eight baselines covering the regimes from Section 2 plus classical anchors: (i) classical (MPC (Falcone et al., 2007), MCTS (Lenz et al., 2016)); (ii) runtime invocation (DriveSpeak (Cui et al., 2024)); (iii) offline extraction (LLaDA (Li et al., 2024a), DriReg (Cai et al., 2024), Plan-R1 (Tang et al., 2025)); (iv) symbolic/hybrid (PDDL (Guan et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023), SymAgent (Liu et al., 2025)). All methods share the observation space, action space, episodes, and LLM backbone (GPT-4o, temperature 0); descriptions, the shared and unshared conditions, and a matched re-run of PDDL and DriReg over REINS’s vocabulary and calibration pipeline are in Appendices B.3 and D.2.

5.2 Performance Evaluation

Performance evaluation results are reported in Table 1, with trajectory accuracy analysis in Appendix C.2.

Effectiveness Analysis. (i) REINS beats all baselines, improving over Plan-R1 by 2.4%–3.6% Compl., 3.06–5.48 RE, and 49%–56% CR reduction—validating that grounding, verification, and consolidation act jointly. (ii) All methods incur higher CR on complex scenarios (Roundabout, Intersection) than structured ones (Highway, Merge); REINS degrades least, owing to context-aware retrieval. (iii) On highD and rounD, REINS maintains Compl. above 0.98 with 6.6–9.0-point CR reduction over Plan-R1, transferring to naturalistic driving without domain-specific tuning. (iv) Executable rule methods (PDDL, DriReg, SymAgent, Plan-R1) beat language-guided ones (DriveSpeak, LLaDA, with 22%–44% CR for ungrounded rules), yet their static thresholds and uniform activation still trail REINS’s data-driven calibration and variable-indexed retrieval; a matched re-run over REINS’s vocabulary and calibration narrows PDDL’s and DriReg’s CR by 3–5 points but leaves the gap intact (Appendix D.2). (v) Classical planners (MPC, MCTS) are fast but unsafe (CR 14%–28%); Plan-R1 is the best baseline but plateaus under uniform rule application.

Efficiency Analysis. REINS completes planning in 1.9–4.6 ms per step, up to 58% faster than runtime LLM baselines (DriveSpeak, LLaDA) and 15–33% faster than Plan-R1. Two factors contribute: (i) variable-indexed retrieval activates only 2–3 rules per step via O⁡(log⁡|ℛ|)O(\log|\mathcal{R}|) queries, and (ii) learned dynamics enable closed-form rollout without iterative LLM calls. PDDL makes no runtime LLM call either, yet re-grounds every precondition at each step (3.71 of its 4.95 ms on Highway; Appendix D.3), exactly the cost that indexed consolidation removes.

5.3 Ablation Study

We conduct ablation experiments on all four simulated scenarios to evaluate component contributions. Table 2 reports results for four variants: (i) w/o World Model: replacing learned dynamics with constant-velocity propagation; (ii) w/o LLM Prior: using purely data-driven structure learning without semantic guidance; (iii) w/o Rule Generation: substituting LLM-generated rules with hand-crafted ones; (iv) w/o Retrieval: applying all rules uniformly without context-aware selection.

Removing the world dynamics model causes the largest safety degradation (CR +49%/+48% on Highway/Intersection), confirming multi-step prediction is essential. Without LLM priors, CR rises 31–46%, showing that semantic guidance regularizes dependency discovery beyond purely data-driven methods. Hand-crafted rules yield the largest compliance drop (0.9956→\to0.9312 on Highway) and nearly double CR, exposing the limited coverage of manual engineering; even so, they remain safer inside the harness than every matched no-harness baseline (Appendix D.2). Disabling context-aware retrieval raises both CR (22–43%) and PE (34–58%) via conflicting constraints. The four roles are complementary: dynamics enables predictive verification, LLM priors regularize structure, rule generation ensures coverage, and selective retrieval prevents conflicts.

5.4 Self-Evolution Analysis

We deploy REINS for 1000 episodes on Highway from the offline-compiled memory ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} (|ℛ0|=88|\mathcal{R}_{0}|{=}88), reporting four checkpoint snapshots alongside a Frozen ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} control that runs the same window with acquisition disabled (Table 3; other scenarios in Appendix C.5). Across deployment, |ℛ||\mathcal{R}| grows from 88 to 145 (saturating after ep. 500; Eq. 9), the LLM call rate decays from 70.0% to 12.81% (a 5.5×\times reduction with no weight update), Compl. rises from 0.9885 to 0.9956, and CR drops from 7.05% to 5.67%. Against the Frozen ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} control over the same horizon (0.9800 Compl., 9.63% CR), online acquisition adds +0.0156+0.0156 Compl. and removes 3.96 CR points—the headline self-evolution gain. Mapped to the three couplings: monotone |ℛ||\mathcal{R}| under κ\kappa-hash deduplication validates consolidation, the joint Compl. ↑\uparrow/CR ↓\downarrow trajectory validates rollout-based verification, and the 5.5×\times call-rate drop validates the grounding–consolidation loop, as variable-keyed memory hits replace LLM calls on similar scenes.

Of the roughly 39,000 proposals implied by these call rates, 2.1% failed schema validation, 18.0% were rejected by rollout verification, and the accepted remainder deduplicated to 57 unique rules, 54 of which an audit judged consistent with domain guidelines (Appendix D.5).

Robustness, Transfer, and Scalability. Appendix D stresses these results. Rules regenerated with Claude Sonnet 4.5 or Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct keep Highway CR at 5.89% and 6.24% (vs. 5.67%), and prompt paraphrases span 5.58–5.91%. Under 2.5–10% observation noise and 5% frame drops, REINS CR rises to at most 8.14% while Plan-R1 rises to 19.87%. A memory compiled only from highD/rounD starts at an 86.2% call rate on highway-env and recovers to within 0.5–1.1 CR points of the native memory within 1000 episodes, whereas a frozen transferred memory does not. Inflating the memory to 100,000 rules keeps retrieval under 0.8 ms, and the 1.59 s miss cycle, dominated by the LLM call, runs off the control path behind a 2.6 ms verified fallback.

6 Limitations

Abstraction gap and action interface. The evaluation sits at the tactical decision layer: perception is assumed as clean factored variables, highD and rounD run in replay (reactive-replay variant in Appendix D.6), and occlusion, tracking, and map errors are absent; the five meta-actions are the standard interface of this layer and of all eight baselines, and continuous maneuvers would change only the scorer’s output head. The claims are harness results at this layer, not a deployable AV stack, and the episode-level collision rates of 5.7–9.5% in deliberately stressed traffic are not deployment grade; the supported claim is relative (49–56% below the best learned baseline). Correlational dynamics. The learned dynamics are prior-constrained but not causally identified; verification is conservative, so misattribution degrades toward rejecting actions rather than accepting unsafe ones, yet its quality depends on dynamics fidelity (constant-velocity propagation raises CR by 48–49%; 3 of the 57 acquired rules were over-specific in audit, Appendix D.5). Limited zero-shot cross-domain reusability. Zero-shot cross-domain reusability of the compiled memory is limited: a memory compiled solely from highD/rounD begins at an 86.2% call rate on highway-env, indicating that many target-domain encounters still require online acquisition. REINS is accordingly scoped to the self-evolution loop rather than assuming universal cross-domain memory transfer (Appendix D.7). Scope. The monotone miss-rate property assumes a stationary scene distribution, and the implementation is specialized to driving: only the variable schema and the action space must be re-authored for another domain (Appendix D.1).

7 Conclusion

We present REINS, a self-evolving agent harness that adapts the agent-harness paradigm from software engineering to real-time, safety-critical trajectory planning through three LLM–planner couplings: grounding, verification, and consolidation. Familiar scenes resolve from an indexed rule memory in 𝒪⁡(log⁡|ℛ|)\mathcal{O}(\log|\mathcal{R}|) time, while memory misses trigger LLM-driven rule acquisition that grounds, verifies, and writes back new rules, closing the self-evolution loop without any LLM weight update. At the tactical decision layer, REINS attains 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9–4.6 ms latency, with gains that survive matched baselines, observation noise, reactive replay, and cross-domain memory transfer. Future work will couple the harness to perception uncertainty and continuous maneuvers, extend it to multi-agent coordination, and move the learned dynamics toward interventional identification with incremental updates.
