Appendix A More Details about REINS

A.1 Variable Definitions

We define macro and micro variables shown in Table 4. The macro variables represent high-level semantic categories, while micro variables are the specific measurable quantities used in the world dynamics model and rule system.

The variables are organized into five functional groups: Environment variables capture external conditions (weather, visibility, road surface, speed limits) that affect driving but are not directly controllable. Traffic variables describe spatial and temporal relationships with surrounding vehicles, including headway distances, relative speeds, TTC, and lane density metrics. Ego variables represent the controlled vehicle’s kinematic state (position, velocity, acceleration, orientation). Action defines the discrete action space: five high-level maneuvers executed by low-level controllers. Outcome variables measure action consequences, including safety (collision risk), comfort (jerk-based), and task completion indicators. This hierarchical organization enables structured rule retrieval via variable-group indexing.

The macro-group dependency set ℰℋ\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}} in Def. 3.1 encodes the admissible group-level edges:

ℰℋ={\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}}=\{ (Env,Traffic),(Env,Ego),(Env,Outcome),\displaystyle(\textsc{Env},\textsc{Traffic}),(\textsc{Env},\textsc{Ego}),(\textsc{Env},\textsc{Outcome}), (10)
(Traffic,Traffic),(Traffic,Ego),(Traffic,Outcome),\displaystyle(\textsc{Traffic},\textsc{Traffic}),(\textsc{Traffic},\textsc{Ego}),(\textsc{Traffic},\textsc{Outcome}),
(Ego,Traffic),(Ego,Ego),(Ego,Outcome),\displaystyle(\textsc{Ego},\textsc{Traffic}),(\textsc{Ego},\textsc{Ego}),(\textsc{Ego},\textsc{Outcome}),
(Action,Ego),(Action,Outcome)}.\displaystyle(\textsc{Action},\textsc{Ego}),(\textsc{Action},\textsc{Outcome})\}.

Environment factors influence Traffic, Ego, and Outcome; Traffic and Ego variables interact bidirectionally and feed into Outcome; Action affects only Ego state and Outcome.

A.2 Rule Templates

Seven rule templates are defined to capture different logical structures for driving knowledge:

  • •

    IF-THEN: Conditional implication for basic conditional relations.
    Example: IF TTC << 2s THEN decelerate

  • •

    AND-THEN: Conjunctive trigger requiring multiple conditions.
    Example: IF visibility << 50m AND raining THEN reduce_speed_by_30%

  • •

    THRESHOLD: Numeric constraint with calibrated boundaries.
    Example: IF speed >> speed_limit THEN violation = true

  • •

    PRIORITY: Decision hierarchy for conflicting actions.
    Example: yield ≻\succ accelerate (yield takes priority)

  • •

    MULTI-ACTION: Compound actions under one condition.
    Example: IF collision_risk = high THEN brake AND steer_away

  • •

    WEIGHTED-ACTION: Weighted action selection.
    Example: IF crash_risk THEN {brake: 0.7, steer: 0.3}

  • •

    TEMPORAL-CHAIN: Temporal constraints between triggers.
    Example: IF obstacle_detected THEN brake within 1.5s

A.3 Rule Conflict Resolution

When multiple rules are activated simultaneously, conflicts may arise if they recommend different actions. REINS resolves conflicts through a three-level arbitration mechanism:

Priority-based ordering. Rules are assigned priority levels based on their functional category: Safety >> Compliance >> Navigation >> Efficiency. When rules from different categories conflict, the higher-priority rule takes precedence. For example, if an Efficiency rule (consider lane change) and a Safety rule (maintain gap) both fire, the Safety rule overrides.

Confidence-weighted aggregation. For rules within the same priority level, REINS aggregates their scores using the noisy-OR formula (Eq. (5)). This allows multiple supporting rules to reinforce an action while remaining robust to individual noisy predictions. The action with the highest aggregated probability is selected.

Dynamics-based verification. When the aggregated action prior is below a confidence threshold (τ=0.7\tau=0.7), REINS falls back to dynamics-based verification. The top-MM candidate actions are simulated via forward rollout using the world dynamics model, and the action yielding the safest predicted trajectory is selected.

This hierarchical approach ensures that safety-critical rules are never overridden by efficiency considerations, while still allowing flexible action selection in non-critical situations.

A.4 Method Details

This subsection contains the full equations, architectural details, and explanatory prose deferred from the methodology to keep the main body concise. The structure mirrors Section 4.1–4.2.

A.4.1 World Dynamics Learning Details

We learn the dependency graph 𝒢^=(𝒳,ℰ^,w^)\hat{\mathcal{G}}=(\mathcal{X},\hat{\mathcal{E}},\hat{w}) in three steps, then train a per-variable dynamics function on the resulting parent sets.

Step 1: Edge Prior Estimation. We query the LLM with variable dependency prompts (Appendix A.5) to obtain an edge confidence πi​j∈[0,1]\pi_{ij}\in[0,1] for each candidate edge Xj→XiX_{j}\to X_{i}. This is combined with the macro-group constraints (Eq. 10) to form a unified prior:

π~i​j=απi​j+(1−α)𝕀{(h(Xj),h(Xi))∈ℰℋ},\tilde{\pi}_{ij}=\alpha\,\pi_{ij}+(1-\alpha)\,\mathbb{I}\{(h(X_{j}),h(X_{i}))\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}}\}, (11)

where α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] balances LLM confidence against structural constraints. Edges that violate the macro-group constraints carry indicator 00 and are reduced to α​πi​j\alpha\,\pi_{ij}, while semantically aligned edges are pushed toward 11.

Step 2: Prior-Guided Regression. For each target variable XiX_{i}, we predict its value from the lagged values of other variables via ridge regression [Hoerl and Kennard, 1970] with prior-adaptive penalties λi​j=λ0​(1−π~i​j)ρ\lambda_{ij}=\lambda_{0}(1-\tilde{\pi}_{ij})^{\rho}:

𝐰^i=arg⁡min⁡∑t=LN𝐰⁡(Xit−∑j≠i∑ℓ=1Lwj​ℓ​Xjt−ℓ)2+∑j≠iλi​j​‖𝐰j‖22,\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{i}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{w}}\sum_{t=L}^{N}\Big(X_{i}^{t}-\textstyle\sum_{j\neq i}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}w_{j\ell}X_{j}^{t-\ell}\Big)^{2}+\sum_{j\neq i}\lambda_{ij}\|\mathbf{w}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}, (12)

where wj​ℓw_{j\ell} is the regression coefficient for variable XjX_{j} at lag ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\}, 𝐰j=(wj​1,…,wj​L)⊤\mathbf{w}_{j}=(w_{j1},\ldots,w_{jL})^{\top} groups all lags for XjX_{j}, λ0\lambda_{0} is the base penalty, and ρ>0\rho>0 controls penalty sharpness. High-prior edges (π~i​j→1\tilde{\pi}_{ij}\to 1) receive weak regularization and survive; low-prior edges are shrunk toward zero.

Step 3: Graph Construction. The parent set Pa⁡(Xi)\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i}) retains the top-KK variables ranked by aggregated coefficient magnitude ∑ℓ=1L|w^j​ℓ|\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}|\hat{w}_{j\ell}|. The learned edge set and weights are

ℰ^={(Xj,Xi)∣Xj∈Pa⁡(Xi)},w^​(Xj,Xi)=∑ℓ=1L|w^j​ℓ|.\hat{\mathcal{E}}=\{(X_{j},X_{i})\mid X_{j}\in\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i})\},\quad\hat{w}(X_{j},X_{i})=\textstyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}|\hat{w}_{j\ell}|. (13)

Dynamics Function Loss. Given 𝒢^\hat{\mathcal{G}}, each fif_{i} is implemented as a multi-head Transformer [Vaswani et al., 2017] and trained by mean squared error over its parent trajectory:

ℒdyn(i)=1N∑t(Xit+1−fi(Pa(Xi)t−L+1:t))2.\mathcal{L}_{\text{dyn}}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t}\big(X_{i}^{t+1}-f_{i}(\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i})^{t-L+1:t})\big)^{2}. (14)

Optimizer, batch size, and convergence curves are reported in Appendix C.1.

A.4.2 Rule Compilation Details

Rule Structure Generation. For each dependency edge (Xj,Xi)∈ℰ^(X_{j},X_{i})\in\hat{\mathcal{E}}, the LLM generates a rule structure

r=(T,𝒫r,ar,cr),r=(T,\mathcal{P}_{r},a_{r},c_{r}), (15)

where TT is the rule template (Def. 3.5), 𝒫r\mathcal{P}_{r} is a set of guard predicates with symbolic thresholds, ar∈𝒜a_{r}\in\mathcal{A} is the recommended action (Def. 3.2), and crc_{r} is the confidence derived from edge weight w^​(Xj,Xi)\hat{w}(X_{j},X_{i}). Prompt details are in Appendix A.5.

Threshold Calibration. Each predicate p∈𝒫rp\in\mathcal{P}_{r} (Def. 3.4) requires a concrete threshold τi\tau_{i}, calibrated from 𝒟\mathcal{D} in three forms [Luo et al., 2024]:

τi={μi+ζ​σi(z-score),Qi​(ζ)(quantile),τ0(absolute),\tau_{i}=\begin{cases}\mu_{i}+\zeta\sigma_{i}&\text{(z-score)},\\ Q_{i}(\zeta)&\text{(quantile)},\\ \tau_{0}&\text{(absolute)},\end{cases} (16)

where μi,σi\mu_{i},\sigma_{i} are empirical mean and standard deviation of XiX_{i}, Qi​(ζ)Q_{i}(\zeta) is the ζ\zeta-quantile, and τ0\tau_{0} is a fixed constant (e.g., speed limits). The comparison operator ≺\prec is selected to maximize safety separability between the two sides of the threshold under safety outcome y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\} (Section 4.1.2).

Graph Database Storage. Compiled rules are stored in a Neo4j graph database [Webber, 2012] with a variable-indexed schema (Figure 3). Each rule node stores the complete tuple (T,𝒫r,ar,cr)(T,\mathcal{P}_{r},a_{r},c_{r}), where TT is the template type, 𝒫r\mathcal{P}_{r} contains calibrated predicates with concrete thresholds τ\tau and operators ≺\prec, ara_{r} is the recommended action, and crc_{r} is the confidence. Rule nodes connect to variable nodes via TRIGGERS (input variables) and AFFECTS (output variables) edges. This enables O⁡(log⁡|ℛ|)O(\log|\mathcal{R}|) retrieval via parameterized Cypher queries on variables active in the current state. Database statistics are provided in Appendix C.7.1.

A.4.3 Rule-Guided Planning Details

Scene-Aware Rule Retrieval. Given st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}, we identify active variables {Xi}\{X_{i}\} and retrieve context-relevant rules via parameterized Cypher queries [Francis et al., 2018] generated by the LLM (read-only and schema-constrained; Appendix A.5). The retrieval map

G:({Xi},K)⟼ℛt⊆ℛG:(\{X_{i}\},K)\longmapsto\mathcal{R}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{R} (17)

returns up to KK rules ranked by confidence crc_{r}. A rule rr is retrieved if its trigger variables {Xj∣(Xj,r)∈TRIGGERS}\{X_{j}\mid(X_{j},r)\in\texttt{TRIGGERS}\} intersect with the active set {Xi}\{X_{i}\} and the dependency direction satisfies the macro-group constraints ℰℋ\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}}.

Action Scorer Architecture. The Transformer scorer [Liang et al., 2022] takes state encoding 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} and rule embedding 𝐮r\mathbf{u}_{r} and emits relevance and action heads:

𝐡t,r\displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{t,r} =TransformerEnc​([𝐱t;𝐮r]),\displaystyle=\text{TransformerEnc}([\mathbf{x}_{t};\mathbf{u}_{r}]), (18)
Srel​(r,st)\displaystyle S_{\text{rel}}(r,s_{t}) =σ⁡(Decrel​(𝐡t,r))∈[0,1],\displaystyle=\sigma(\text{Dec}_{\text{rel}}(\mathbf{h}_{t,r}))\in[0,1],
Sact​(r,st,a)\displaystyle S_{\text{act}}(r,s_{t},a) =softmax​(Decact​(𝐡t,r))a,\displaystyle=\mathrm{softmax}(\text{Dec}_{\text{act}}(\mathbf{h}_{t,r}))_{a},

where SrelS_{\text{rel}} predicts whether rr should influence the current decision, and SactS_{\text{act}} predicts the action preference given rr. The combined rule-action score multiplies relevance, action preference, and rule confidence:

f⁡(r,a∣st)=Srel​(r,st)⋅Sact​(r,st,a)⋅cr.f(r,a\mid s_{t})=S_{\text{rel}}(r,s_{t})\cdot S_{\text{act}}(r,s_{t},a)\cdot c_{r}. (19)

Scorer Training. The scorer is trained on expert trajectories {(st,at∗)}\{(s_{t},a^{*}_{t})\} with a joint relevance + action objective:

ℒ=∑t,r[BCE⁡(Exec⁡(r,st),Srel​(r,st))−log⁡Sact​(r,st,at∗)],\mathcal{L}=\sum_{t,r}\big[\mathrm{BCE}(\mathrm{Exec}(r,s_{t}),S_{\text{rel}}(r,s_{t}))-\log S_{\text{act}}(r,s_{t},a^{*}_{t})\big], (20)

where Exec⁡(r,st)∈{0,1}\mathrm{Exec}(r,s_{t})\in\{0,1\} is the ground-truth rule activation (Eq. 2) and at∗a^{*}_{t} is the expert action.

Action Aggregation. The full noisy-OR action distribution corresponding to Eq. 5 is

P⁡(a∣st)\displaystyle P(a\mid s_{t}) =1−∏r∈ℛt​(a)(1−f⁡(r,a∣st))Z,\displaystyle=\frac{1-\prod_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{t}(a)}\big(1-f(r,a\mid s_{t})\big)}{Z}, (21)
arule∗\displaystyle a^{*}_{\text{rule}} =arg⁡maxa∈𝒜⁡P⁡(a∣st),\displaystyle=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}P(a\mid s_{t}),

where ℛt​(a)⊆ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t}(a)\subseteq\mathcal{R}_{t} denotes the rules with recommended action ar=aa_{r}=a and ZZ normalizes over 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The formulation favors actions supported by multiple high-confidence rules.

Trajectory Verification. For the top-MM actions ranked by P⁡(a∣st)P(a\mid s_{t}), we predict HH-step future states:

s^t+h+1=Φ(s^t+h,a;𝒢^,ℱ^),h=0,…,H−1,\hat{s}_{t+h+1}=\Phi(\hat{s}_{t+h},a;\hat{\mathcal{G}},\hat{\mathcal{F}}),\quad h=0,\ldots,H-1, (22)

where Φ\Phi applies each fi∈ℱ^f_{i}\in\hat{\mathcal{F}} to predict XiX_{i} from Pa⁡(Xi)\mathrm{Pa}(X_{i}) under 𝒢^\hat{\mathcal{G}}. Each rollout produces a candidate trajectory ξ^​(a)=(s^t+1,…,s^t+H)\hat{\xi}(a)=(\hat{s}_{t+1},\ldots,\hat{s}_{t+H}), consistent with Def. 3.3. The planner selects at⋆=arg⁡maxa∈𝒜M⁡J⁡(ξ^​(a))a^{\star}_{t}=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{M}}J(\hat{\xi}(a)), where J:𝒮H→ℝJ:\mathcal{S}^{H}\to\mathbb{R} penalizes collisions, rule violations, and control effort (Appendix B.2); the first control of the selected trajectory is executed in receding-horizon [Zhang et al., 2021b].

A.4.4 Online Rule Acquisition Details

LLM-Driven Rule Proposal. On a miss, the harness queries ℳ\mathcal{M} with the current state and active variables:

r~=(T~,𝒫~,a~,c~)∼ℳ⁡(st),\tilde{r}=(\tilde{T},\tilde{\mathcal{P}},\tilde{a},\tilde{c})\;\sim\;\mathcal{M}(s_{t}), (23)

where r~\tilde{r} conforms to the rule template (Def. 3.5) and uses only variables in 𝒳\mathcal{X} and operators from the predicate grammar (Def. 3.4). Prompt details are in Appendix A.5.

Safe-Action Selection. When online rule acquisition rejects r~\tilde{r} and ℛt=∅\mathcal{R}_{t}=\emptyset, the harness raises a human-takeover alert and executes the action that maximizes minimum lookahead time-to-collision under ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}}:

atsafe=arg⁡maxa∈𝒜​minh∈[1,H]⁡TTC⁡(s^t+h​(a)).a^{\mathrm{safe}}_{t}=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\;\min_{h\in[1,H]}\mathrm{TTC}\!\left(\hat{s}_{t+h}(a)\right). (24)

Memory-Update Collision Branch. Eq. 8’s collision branch averages confidences instead of creating a duplicate node, so |ℛ||\mathcal{R}| counts distinct rule structures rather than LLM-noise replicas. The hash κ\kappa is computed over the structural triple (T~,𝒫~,a~)(\tilde{T},\tilde{\mathcal{P}},\tilde{a}) but excludes c~\tilde{c}, so semantically identical proposals collide regardless of confidence noise. Collisions are common during early deployment when ℛ\mathcal{R} is small, then taper off as coverage saturates.

Self-Evolution Properties. Eq. 8 structurally enforces |ℛt+1|≥|ℛt||\mathcal{R}_{t+1}|\geq|\mathcal{R}_{t}| (memory monotonicity) and θℳ≡θℳ(0)\theta_{\mathcal{M}}\equiv\theta_{\mathcal{M}}^{(0)} (no LLM parameter update). Under stationarity of the scene distribution, the per-state miss rate is non-increasing as ℛ\mathcal{R} accumulates coverage, since any state ss that triggered a miss and produced an accepted r~\tilde{r} is now matched by a rule keyed on the variables active at ss. Since ℳ\mathcal{M} is invoked only on misses, its per-scene invocation rate decays monotonically with Pr⁡[Miss]\Pr[\mathrm{Miss}]. We validate this behavior empirically in Section 5.4 and Appendix C.5.

A.5 Prompts

We provide three prompt templates used in REINS’s offline compilation pipeline. Figure 4 shows the Variable Dependency Prompt, which instructs the LLM to infer dependencies between driving variables based on domain knowledge; the output serves as semantic priors for structure learning in the world dynamics model. Figure 5 presents the Rule Extraction Prompt, which converts dependency edges into executable driving rules with parameterized guards and discrete actions; these rules are stored in the Neo4j graph database. Figure 6 displays the Parameterized Cypher Query Prompt, which generates parameterized queries for context-aware rule retrieval during planning. All prompts enforce read-only constraints and structured output formats to ensure safety and parseability.

Appendix B Implementation Details

B.1 Experiment Settings

Table 5 summarizes the key hyperparameters and training configurations used in our experiments. The settings are organized into six categories: Simulation Environment specifies the highway-env simulator settings, including four driving scenarios with varying complexity and a discrete action space of five high-level maneuvers. Real-world Datasets describes the highD (highway) and rounD (roundabout) drone datasets used for real-world evaluation, including recording statistics and sampling rates. World Dynamics Model details the structure learning parameters (LLM prior weight, regularization) and neural network architecture (Transformer layers, attention heads). Rule Compilation covers the offline LLM-based rule generation process, including the backbone model, sampling strategy, and threshold calibration. Training & Evaluation specifies the data splits, random seeds, and hardware configuration. Planning & Deployment reports inference-time parameters and latency measurements demonstrating real-time capability. All hyperparameter configurations follow standard practices unless otherwise stated.

B.2 Evaluation Metrics

Rule Compliance (Compl.) measures the fraction of timesteps where all active rules are satisfied:

Compl.=1T​∑t=1T∏k=1K(1−vk,t),\text{Compl.}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\prod_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(1-v_{k,t}\bigr), (25)

where vk,t∈{0,1}v_{k,t}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether rule kk is violated at time tt.

Collision Rate (CR) measures the fraction of episodes in which at least one collision occurs:

CR=1N​∑i=1N𝕀⁡(collision in episode ​i),\text{CR}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(\text{collision in episode }i), (26)

where NN is the number of test episodes. A lower CR indicates safer planning.

Risk-aware Efficiency (RE) balances task performance against safety:

RE =Rtask​(τ)−λrisk​Rrisk​(τ),\displaystyle=R_{\text{task}}(\tau)-\lambda_{\text{risk}}R_{\text{risk}}(\tau), (27)
Rrisk​(τ)\displaystyle R_{\text{risk}}(\tau) =∑t=1Tmax⁡(0,δttc−TTCt),\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\max(0,\delta_{\text{ttc}}-\text{TTC}_{t}), (28)

where RtaskR_{\text{task}} is the task reward, RriskR_{\text{risk}} penalizes low TTC states, λrisk=0.5\lambda_{\text{risk}}=0.5 is the risk penalty weight, and δttc=3.0\delta_{\text{ttc}}=3.0s is the TTC threshold.

Planning Efficiency (PE) measures average computation time per decision:

PE=1T​∑t=1Ttplan,\text{PE}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}t_{\text{plan}}, (29)

where tplant_{\text{plan}} (ms) is the wall-clock time for action selection.

Trajectory Objective J⁡(ξ^)J(\hat{\xi}). The trajectory-level objective used in dynamics-based verification is defined as:

J⁡(ξ^)\displaystyle J(\hat{\xi}) =∑h=1Hγh−1[−λsafe⋅𝕀(TTCt+h<τttc)\displaystyle=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\gamma^{h-1}\Big[-\lambda_{\text{safe}}\cdot\mathbb{I}(\text{TTC}_{t+h}<\tau_{\text{ttc}}) (30)
+λprog⋅Δdt+h−λcomf⋅|jt+h|],\displaystyle+\lambda_{\text{prog}}\cdot\Delta d_{t+h}-\lambda_{\text{comf}}\cdot|j_{t+h}|\Big],

where TTCt+h\text{TTC}_{t+h} is the predicted time-to-collision, Δ​dt+h\Delta d_{t+h} is the progress toward the goal, jt+hj_{t+h} is the jerk, and τttc=2.0\tau_{\text{ttc}}=2.0s is the safety threshold. The weights λsafe=1.0\lambda_{\text{safe}}=1.0, λprog=0.5\lambda_{\text{prog}}=0.5, λcomf=0.1\lambda_{\text{comf}}=0.1 prioritize safety over progress and comfort.

Real-world Evaluation Protocol. We use closed-loop replay: one recorded vehicle is controlled by the planner while others follow recorded trajectories. Collisions are detected when bounding boxes overlap or the ego deviates beyond lane boundaries. In the simulated scenarios the surrounding vehicles instead react to the ego (IDM with MOBIL); a reactive-replay variant of highD is reported in Appendix D.6.

B.3 Baseline Descriptions

We select baselines from three categories to comprehensively evaluate REINS: (i) classical planners (MPC, MCTS) that represent traditional optimization and search-based approaches without rule guidance; (ii) LLM-based planners (DriveSpeak, PDDL, LLaDA, DriReg) that leverage language models for driving decisions but differ in how they integrate linguistic knowledge; and (iii) hybrid methods (SymAgent, Plan-R1) that combine learning with symbolic reasoning. This selection covers the spectrum from rule-free to rule-guided planning, enabling analysis of how different rule representation and retrieval strategies affect safety and efficiency.

  • •

    MPC [Falcone et al., 2007]: Classical optimization-based planner solving finite-horizon control under kinematic and safety constraints. We use a 5-step horizon with quadratic cost on acceleration and jerk.

  • •

    MCTS [Lenz et al., 2016]: Sampling-based planning via tree search and rollout evaluation. We use 1000 simulations per decision with UCB exploration.

  • •

    DriveSpeak [Cui et al., 2024]: LLM-based method mapping natural-language scene descriptions directly to driving actions. Uses GPT-4o with scene prompts at each timestep.

  • •

    PDDL [Guan et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2023]: the LLM writes the domain’s symbolic preconditions and effects once offline; at runtime a classical STRIPS solver (Pyperplan [Alkhazraji et al., 2020]) is invoked in process at each decision step with no LLM call. Its runtime profile is in Appendix D.3.

  • •

    LLaDA [Li et al., 2024a]: LLM interpretation of region-specific traffic rules from driver handbooks. Uses pre-extracted rule sets with LLM-based rule matching.

  • •

    DriReg [Cai et al., 2024]: RAG-based traffic regulation retrieval with LLM reasoning for action legality. Retrieves top-5 regulations per query using embedding similarity.

  • •

    SymAgent [Liu et al., 2025]: Neural-symbolic agent integrating LLMs with structured knowledge graphs. Uses the same Neo4j backend as REINS for fair comparison.

  • •

    Plan-R1 [Tang et al., 2025]: Two-stage learning-based planner with rule-shaped rewards and reinforcement learning. Trained on the same 50k episodes as REINS’s world model.

All baselines use identical observation spaces, action spaces, episodes, and evaluation protocols. For LLM-based methods, we use GPT-4o (2024-08-06) with temperature 0 for deterministic outputs. Hyperparameters for each baseline follow their original papers or are tuned on a held-out validation set. The conditions that are shared with REINS and those that each rule-based baseline keeps by design, together with a matched re-run and a common-reference compliance audit, are documented in Appendix D.2.

Appendix C Additional Results

C.1 Training Convergence

We train the world dynamics model for 300 epochs using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} and batch size 64. Each variable-specific dynamics function fif_{i} is implemented as a two-layer Transformer with four attention heads. Training is conducted on 50k episodes collected from four scenarios (Highway, Intersection, Merge, and Roundabout) using NVIDIA A100 GPUs. The model learns 20 variable-specific dynamics functions, including ego-state variables (ego_speed, ego_acceleration, ego_vx, ego_vy, ego_x, ego_y, yaw_rate, jerk, lane_id), traffic-related variables (lead_ttc, lead_thw, lead_rel_speed, rear_rel_speed, lane_density_left, lane_density_right, cutin_risk), and outcome variables (risk_score, comfort_score, violation_flag, energy_consumption). Figure 7 shows the training loss curves for all dynamics functions across the four scenarios.

The results suggest that the learned world dynamics are scenario-adaptive not only in difficulty but also in structural composition: different scenarios activate and learn different subsets of variable-specific dynamics functions. Interaction-heavy variables such as cutin_risk, lane_density_left/right, and rear_rel_speed are prominent in Merge and Intersection, where lane changes and merging behaviors are frequent, but are weakly activated or effectively absent in Highway, where traffic flow is comparatively stable. Conversely, lateral-motion variables (e.g., ego_vy, yaw_rate) become substantially more relevant in Roundabout due to persistent curvature, while contributing marginally in straight-road scenarios. This indicates that the model does not impose a fixed global mechanism set across environments, but instead learns scenario-specific mechanism structures, supporting structural adaptability to heterogeneous traffic contexts.

Beyond these structural differences, the loss curves exhibit consistent convergence patterns. Most variables converge within 100–150 epochs. Simple kinematic variables (e.g., ego_x, ego_y, lead_thw) converge within 50 epochs, whereas interaction-intensive outcome variables (e.g., risk_score, violation_flag) require longer training. Highway achieves the lowest final loss due to simpler lane-following dynamics. Roundabout exhibits higher loss for lateral variables because of curved trajectories, while Intersection shows higher variance in violation_flag due to diverse right-of-way interactions. Safety-related variables (e.g., lead_ttc, cutin_risk) converge rapidly in early training when relevant interactions are present, indicating strong dependency signals. In terms of final loss magnitude, continuous variables (e.g., ego_speed, ego_acceleration) achieve losses below 0.5, whereas discrete or binary variables (e.g., violation_flag, lane_id) stabilize at higher loss due to their classification nature.

C.2 Trajectory Accuracy

We evaluate trajectory accuracy using Average Displacement Error (ADE), Final Displacement Error (FDE), and cumulative episode reward (Reward) across four driving scenarios: Highway, Merge, Roundabout, and Intersection. ADE and FDE measure the mean and final Euclidean distance between predicted and executed trajectories, respectively, while Reward reflects overall driving efficiency and safety. All methods are evaluated under identical environment settings with the same observation space, action space, and rollout horizon.

Table 6 reports the mean performance over all evaluation episodes. REINS consistently achieves the best performance across all scenarios in terms of both trajectory accuracy and cumulative reward. In Highway, REINS reduces ADE and FDE to 15.9 and 20.5, respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline (SymAgent) by 12.2% in ADE and 16.3% in FDE, while also achieving the highest reward. Similar improvements are observed in Merge and Roundabout, where REINS yields substantial gains in both short-horizon and long-horizon prediction accuracy, indicating more stable multi-step trajectory generation.

The performance gap becomes more pronounced in complex interaction scenarios. In Intersection, REINS achieves an ADE of 5.6 and FDE of 9.7, representing relative reductions of 30.0% and 13.4% compared to SymAgent, and 41.7% (ADE) and 28.7% (FDE) compared to MPC. This suggests that integrating rule-guided action selection with world-model-based forward rollout is particularly effective when decision-making requires anticipating multi-agent interactions and right-of-way constraints.

Across all scenarios, higher trajectory accuracy strongly correlates with higher episode reward, confirming that more accurate future state prediction leads to safer and more efficient planning. Methods relying primarily on language-based reasoning (LLaDA) exhibit the largest errors, especially in high-speed or curved-road settings, highlighting the limitations of planning without explicit dynamics modeling. MPC improves performance by incorporating learned motion predictors, while SymAgent further benefits from symbolic constraints. REINS combines symbolic rule guidance with learned world dynamics, enabling both structured action filtering and predictive verification, which explains its consistent superiority across heterogeneous traffic scenarios.

C.3 Sensitivity to Retrieval Count kk and Planning Horizon HH

We analyze sensitivity to two runtime hyperparameters: rule retrieval count kk (the maximum number of rules returned per scene by the Cypher query) and planning horizon HH (the rollout depth used by trajectory verification). Both are evaluated on simulated (Highway, Roundabout) and real-world (highD, rounD) scenarios.

Rule Retrieval Count kk. Table 9(a) reports results for varying kk. Small values (k≤3k\!\leq\!3) miss critical rules, increasing CR by 3.5–4.7 points; large values (k≥15k\!\geq\!15) introduce redundancy, raising PE by 60–71% at k=20k{=}20 without safety gains. The optimal k=10k{=}10 generalizes across domains, with real-world and roundabout scenarios showing higher sensitivity than structured highway settings.

Planning Horizon HH. Table 9(b) reports results for varying HH. Short horizons (H≤3H\!\leq\!3) cause myopic decisions with 2.9–5.1 point CR increase; long horizons raise PE by 35–44% at H=7H{=}7 and roughly double it at H=10H{=}10, with marginal safety benefits. The optimal H=5H{=}5 balances safety and efficiency, though complex scenarios (Roundabout, rounD) require longer horizons to anticipate multi-agent interactions.

C.4 Sensitivity to Temporal Lag Length

The temporal lag length LL determines how many historical timesteps the world dynamics model uses when predicting future states. Table 7 reports results on both simulated and real-world scenarios.

When using small lag lengths (L≤2L\leq 2), the model fails to capture cumulative temporal patterns such as sustained tailgating or gradual lane drift, leading to substantially higher collision rates. On the simulated Highway scenario, the collision rate increases from 5.67% at L=6L=6 to 9.34%, corresponding to a 65% relative increase. A similar degradation is observed on the real-world highD dataset, where the collision rate rises from 6.12% to 10.12%. These results indicate that short-term observations are insufficient to infer latent interaction states, such as risk accumulation and driver intent, which are critical for safe planning. In contrast, large lag lengths (L≥10L\geq 10) introduce excessive historical noise and dilute recent dependency signals, reducing the effective signal-to-noise ratio for short-horizon prediction. Consequently, collision rates increase by approximately 40% on simulated scenarios compared to the optimal setting. This suggests that overly long histories may impair the model’s ability to focus on immediately relevant dynamics, particularly in rapidly evolving traffic situations.

Overall, L=6L=6 achieves the best and most consistent performance across both simulated and real-world domains, corresponding to approximately 1.2 seconds of historical context at a sampling rate of 5 Hz. This time window appears sufficient to capture short-term interaction dynamics while avoiding the accumulation of outdated or irrelevant information, thereby supporting stable multi-step rollout and reliable safety verification in downstream planning.

C.5 Self-Evolution Across Scenarios

This appendix reports self-evolution dynamics on the remaining simulated scenarios (Merge, Roundabout, Intersection) and the real-world datasets (highD, rounD), complementing the Highway results in Section 5.4. For each scenario, we deploy REINS for 1000 episodes from the offline-compiled memory ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} and report |ℛ||\mathcal{R}|, LLM call rate, Compl., and CR at four deployment checkpoints (ep. 250, 500, 750, 1000), with a Frozen ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} row showing the same 1000-episode window run with acquisition disabled; this row exposes |ℛ0||\mathcal{R}_{0}| and isolates the contribution of online rule writing from any aggregation effect of running more episodes. The per-scenario |ℛ||\mathcal{R}| at ep. 1000 matches the post-deployment totals in Table 8.

Three patterns emerge across the five extended scenarios, mirroring the Highway dynamics. First, |ℛ||\mathcal{R}| exhibits saturating growth: approximately 44% of the rule additions (counted from |ℛ0||\mathcal{R}_{0}| in the Frozen row to |ℛ||\mathcal{R}| at ep. 1000) occur in the first 250 episodes, with diminishing returns thereafter, so the LLM is invoked predominantly for previously unseen scene clusters. Second, the LLM call rate decays monotonically in all scenarios, from 68–79% in the first 250-episode window to 12–19% by ep. 1000 (a 4.2–5.5×\times reduction); scene complexity raises the absolute size of ℛ\mathcal{R} and the residual call rate (highest on Intersection) but not the shape of the decay. Third, the Frozen ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} control consistently underperforms the evolving memory at ep. 1000 (mean Compl. gap ≈\approx0.017, mean CR gap ≈\approx4.2 points), confirming that the gains attributable to online acquisition are not artifacts of statistical aggregation over a longer evaluation window. Intersection benefits most (Compl. +0.0218+0.0218, CR −4.87-4.87 points from Frozen to ep. 1000), reflecting larger room for online acquisition where the offline ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} is most incomplete relative to right-of-way reasoning; the other four scenarios cluster in a tight range (Compl. +0.0154+0.0154 to +0.0164+0.0164, CR −3.79-3.79 to −4.40-4.40 points). highD mirrors Highway and rounD mirrors Roundabout in both |ℛ||\mathcal{R}| growth shape and Compl./CR convergence, indicating that the harness operates on factored variable signatures rather than scenario-specific surface features. Cross-domain transfer of the compiled memory itself is studied separately in Appendix D.7.

C.6 Case Study

Figure 9 compares trajectories of REINS, Plan-R1, LLaDA, and MPC on two scenarios, with activated rules and actions shown at each timestep. Rule definitions are provided in Appendix C.7.2.

Simulated Highway. REINS activates R03 and R07 at t=0t{=}0 to monitor the lead vehicle and adjacent lanes, triggers R12 at t=0.5t{=}0.5s when a safe gap appears, executes a lane change at t=1.0t{=}1.0s, and accelerates via R15 at t=1.5t{=}1.5s, producing a smooth action sequence (IDLE→\!\to\!IDLE→\!\to\!RIGHT→\!\to\!FASTER). Plan-R1 applies all 15 rules simultaneously, causing conflicting constraints and repeated deceleration (SLOWER×3\!\times\!3) before a delayed maneuver.

Real-World highD. In the cut-in scenario, REINS detects lateral intrusion at t=0t{=}0 via R05, performs preemptive deceleration at t=0.5t{=}0.5s using R07, and maintains safe distance until t=1.5t{=}1.5s (IDLE→\!\to\!SLOWER→\!\to\!SLOWER→\!\to\!IDLE). Plan-R1 responds later with emergency braking at t=1.0t{=}1.0s due to uniform rule execution.

C.7 Compiled Rule Database

C.7.1 Rule Database Statistics

Table 8 shows the distribution of variables by macro-group and rules by template type in REINS’s Neo4j graph database. The post-deployment database contains 1,023 rules covering six driving scenarios (four simulated: Highway, Merge, Roundabout, Intersection; two real-world: highD, rounD). IF-THEN and AND-THEN templates dominate due to the prevalence of conditional and multi-condition reasoning in driving. Intersection scenarios contain the most rules due to complex right-of-way interactions, while Highway scenarios require fewer given simpler lane-following dynamics. This scale is comparable to industrial rule-based systems while remaining tractable for O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) graph database retrieval (<<1 ms per query).

Figure 8 visualizes the graph structure of 200 randomly sampled rules from the database. Gray nodes are variables, blue nodes are rules, and pink nodes are the five discrete actions. Edge colors match source node colors: gray edges represent Variable→\toRule, while blue edges represent Rule→\toAction.

Several structural patterns emerge from this visualization: (1) Variable sharing: A small set of variables (e.g., TTC, THW, speed) triggers a large number of rules, indicating that safety-critical variables serve as common preconditions across diverse driving scenarios. (2) Action concentration: The majority of rules converge to SLOWER and IDLE, which exhibit the highest in-degree among all five actions. This reflects the safety-first design principle where conservative actions are recommended under uncertain or risky conditions. In contrast, LANE_LEFT, LANE_RIGHT, and FASTER receive fewer rule connections, as these actions require more stringent preconditions. (3) Rule diversity: Despite action concentration, rules maintain diverse trigger conditions from different variables, enabling fine-grained context-aware activation rather than uniform rule application. These patterns support REINS’s retrieval strategy: variable-indexed queries efficiently activate relevant rule subsets, while action aggregation via noisy-OR naturally prioritizes safety-critical recommendations.

C.7.2 Representative Rules

Table 11 lists 15 representative rules from REINS’s compiled rule database. The full post-deployment Neo4j database contains 1,023 rules across six driving scenarios, from which context-relevant subsets are retrieved at runtime via parameterized Cypher queries. These rules are automatically compiled from LLM-generated linguistic descriptions and calibrated using the threshold calibration mechanism described in Section 4.1.2. For fair comparison, Plan-R1 applies the same 15 representative rules uniformly at each step, while REINS selectively activates 2–3 context-relevant rules via the retrieval mechanism.

The 15 rules cover six of the seven template types defined in Definition 3.5: (1) THRESHOLD rules (R01, R02, R06) enforce numeric boundaries on physical variables such as TTC and speed; (2) IF-THEN rules (R03, R07) implement basic conditional logic with disjunctive guards; (3) AND-THEN rules (R04, R05, R11–R15) require multiple conditions to be satisfied simultaneously; (4) PRIORITY rules (R09) establish decision hierarchies for right-of-way scenarios; (5) MULTI-ACTION rules (R10) trigger compound actions under critical conditions; (6) TEMPORAL-CHAIN rules (R08) encode time-sensitive constraints for upcoming events. The complete definitions of all seven rule template types are provided in Appendix A.2, and the conflict resolution mechanism is described in Appendix A.3.

Appendix D Fairness Protocol, Robustness, Transfer, and Scalability

This appendix collects the studies that scope the harness claim and stress the main results: the domain-specific versus domain-agnostic components of the harness (D.1), the baseline fairness protocol with a matched re-run and a common-reference compliance audit (D.2), the runtime profile of the PDDL baseline (D.3), robustness to the LLM backbone and to prompt variation (D.4), what rollout verification filters (D.5), reactive replay and observation noise (D.6), cross-domain memory transfer (D.7), the latency of the online-miss cycle and its scheduling (D.8), and retrieval at deployment scale (D.9). Unless stated otherwise, all studies use the Highway scenario, five seeds, and the protocol of Section 5.1.

D.1 Scope of the Harness Claim

The three couplings are presented as a harness pattern, while the implementation is specialized to driving. Table 12 classifies each component of REINS and sketches the instantiation for a different trajectory-planning domain, robot-arm manipulation, whose action space is continuous and high-dimensional and whose safety notions (contact force, grasp stability) differ from driving. Two components are domain schemas that any instantiation must author; the remaining five transfer unchanged. The safety notion enters only through the variable schema and the terms of the objective JJ: calibrated predicates over contact-force variables are structurally identical to TTC guards, and the calibration procedure and the verification protocol do not change. The harness contribution lives in the five unchanged components; the two redesigned ones constitute the domain description that any planner for that domain must author anyway.

D.2 Baseline Fairness Protocol

Shared and unshared conditions. PDDL, DriReg, and LLaDA were conceived for symbolic planning domains, regulatory text, and driver handbooks respectively, none with a factored driving state, so each was re-implemented faithfully to its original design for closed-loop highway-env. Table 13 lists what is shared with REINS and what each method keeps by design. The shared conditions fix the observation space, action space, episodes, LLM backbone, and decoding; the unshared ones leave each method its own knowledge representation and thresholds, which leaves the rule-generation procedure as a confound. Three instruments below isolate the harness regardless.

Matched re-run. We regenerated the PDDL and DriReg rules over the same 44-variable vocabulary, passed their thresholds through REINS’s calibration pipeline, and re-evaluated (Table 14). Input normalization improves both baselines by 3–5 CR points and explains a minority of the gap; the majority survives it.

Bracketing with the ablations. Two ablations from Table 2 bracket the remaining gap with the paper’s own numbers. Hand-crafted rules inside the full harness still reach CR 11.23% on Highway, better than every matched no-harness variant in Table 14 and close to the best baseline Plan-R1 at 12.83%. Conversely, applying REINS’s rules uniformly, the way the baselines use rules, raises CR by 22–43% and PE by 34–58%. Worse inputs with the harness keep most of the gain; the same inputs without the harness lose it.

Common-reference compliance. Compliance in Table 1 is measured against each method’s own rule set. Table 15 re-scores every method against REINS’s compiled rule set as a common reference. Compliance is a property of the executed trajectory rather than of the planner: at each step, the reference rules whose guards hold in the logged state become active, and a violation is counted when the logged behavior fails an active rule (Appendix B.2). Each method therefore plans exactly as before and its trajectories are audited afterward, which is also how the four methods without native rule sets receive values. Because the reference set equals REINS’s planning set, REINS’s own value is unchanged by construction; the informative content is that the baseline ordering and the gaps persist.

D.3 Runtime Profile of the PDDL Baseline

The PDDL baseline follows the pipeline in which the LLM writes the domain’s preconditions and effects offline and a classical solver executes at runtime [Guan et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2023]. The solver is Pyperplan [Alkhazraji et al., 2020], a Python STRIPS planner invoked in process at each decision step; there is no per-step LLM call. Its 4.95 ms per step on Highway (Table 1) decomposes into grounding 3.71 ms, search 0.94 ms, and plan extraction 0.30 ms. The solver re-instantiates every precondition against the current state at every step with no indexing, so grounding takes roughly three quarters of the budget. REINS avoids exactly this cost: variable-indexed retrieval touches 2–3 rules in under 1 ms, followed by a fixed-size rollout at H=5H{=}5. This is the architectural payoff of consolidation with indexing.

D.4 Robustness to the LLM Backbone and to Prompt Variation

The LLM produces the dependency priors, the rule structures, and the Cypher queries, so we regenerate the whole offline pipeline with two further backbones and with three paraphrases of the dependency and rule-extraction prompts (Table 16). Rule structure varies mildly across backbones and paraphrases, while the calibrated thresholds and the final behavior barely move. The LLM picks variables, templates, and actions; calibration re-anchors every numeric threshold to data, so backbone differences wash out at the threshold level. Malformed or unsafe proposals never reach memory, because rollout verification rejects them regardless of which backbone or prompt produced them.

D.5 What Rollout Verification Filters

On the 1000-episode Highway deployment of Section 5.4, applying the windowed call rates of Table 3 to the 100,000 deployment steps yields roughly 39,000 logged proposals (an arithmetic consequence of the call rates, not an independent count). Of these, 2.1% failed schema validation, 18.0% were rejected by rollout verification, and 79.9% were accepted. Acceptances overwhelmingly hash-collide with rules already in memory (Eq. 8) and only update confidences; they deduplicate to the 57 unique rules that grow the memory from 88 to 145. A manual audit of the 57 unique rules judged 54 consistent with domain guidelines; the three flagged rules were over-specific and never activated again. Episodes in which at least one acquired rule fired show no elevated collision rate against episodes in which none fired (5.4% against 5.8%).

Three properties of the design bound what a plausible but incorrect proposal can do. Verification errs toward rejection: a rule is accepted only if every calibrated predicate holds along the predicted horizon (Eq. 7), so dynamics error costs availability rather than safety in the common case. Accepted rules never bypass the runtime loop: every executed action is re-verified by rollout at decision time (Section 4.2.1), so a wrongly accepted rule must also survive the per-step check before it can affect control. Finally, the residual dependence on dynamics fidelity is stated in Section 6.

D.6 Reactive Replay and Observation Noise

Reactive replay. In the four simulated scenarios the surrounding vehicles already react to the ego through IDM car-following with MOBIL lane changes. The real-world rows keep highD and rounD as recorded so that they reflect human behavior rather than a simulator’s. To measure the effect of this choice, a reactive-replay variant on highD switches recorded vehicles within 50 m of the ego to IDM once interaction occurs, following the reactive closed-loop protocol of nuPlan [Caesar et al., 2021]. REINS CR moves from 6.12% to 6.94% while Plan-R1 moves from 12.78% to 15.36%, so the gap to the strongest baseline widens.

Observation noise. We corrupt the observed variables with zero-mean Gaussian noise scaled to each variable’s standard deviation and, separately, drop 5% of frames (Table 17). Calibrated thresholds carry a data-derived margin and every action is vetted by a multi-step rollout rather than by a single reading, so REINS degrades more slowly than the strongest baseline at every level, with Compl. staying at or above 0.987. Full-stack perception errors (occlusion, tracking identity switches, map errors) remain out of scope.

D.7 Cross-Domain Memory Transfer

We test how the memory behaves when the offline data are domain-shifted, using the checkpoint protocol of Table 3. Setting A compiles ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} solely from highD and rounD (whose memories total 187 rules before merging and content-hash deduplication) and deploys on highway-env; Setting B compiles it solely from the four simulated scenarios (432 rules before deduplication) and deploys on highD and rounD. Table 18 reports the ep. 250 and ep. 1000 endpoints of each setting, together with a frozen-transfer control on Highway; the native reference rows come from Table 3 and Table 10.

A domain-shifted memory starts degraded: at ep. 250 the call rate runs 86.2% on Highway against the native 70.0% of Table 3, and CR runs several points above the native value at the same checkpoint (11.84% against 7.05%). Acquisition recovers most of the gap within 1000 episodes: final CR lands within 0.5–1.1 points of native and Compl. within 0.003–0.006. On Highway, freezing the transferred memory prevents recovery: at ep. 1000 the frozen transfer stays at CR 11.20% against 6.21% with acquisition enabled, so the recovery comes from verification-gated acquisition rather than from the transferred rules themselves, mirroring the native pattern of Table 3, where frozen ℛ0\mathcal{R}_{0} ends at CR 9.63% against the evolved 5.67%. Sim-to-real shows slightly smaller residual gaps and lower final call rates than real-to-sim; one plausible factor is its larger source memory (432 against 187 rules before deduplication).

The initial call rate of 86.2% also shows that most of the source-domain memory is not functionally reusable zero-shot in a new but still driving context. This is consistent with the safety-oriented design: thresholds are calibrated to the source-domain distribution, so under shift the harness re-invokes and re-verifies rather than reusing rules whose calibration may no longer hold. We therefore do not frame these results as evidence of strong zero-shot generalization; the limitation is stated in Section 6.

D.8 Latency of the Online-Miss Cycle and Its Scheduling

What PE counts. For every method, PE measures the synchronous action-selection computation per step. In the evaluated closed-loop setting, a miss completes proposal, verification, and write-back within the step while simulation time is paused, so the reported PE excludes the acquisition pipeline, namely the LLM call together with the subsequent parsing, calibration, verification, and write-back. Table 19 profiles each stage.

Deployment scheduling. The cycle takes 1.59 s mean, dominated by the LLM call; the acquisition stages other than the LLM call total about 11 ms. In deployment the cycle moves off the critical path by construction, because the planner has a defined behavior without the acquired rule: the best action over the retrieved rules or, with empty retrieval, the safe action that maximizes minimum lookahead TTC (Eq. 24) together with a human-takeover alert. The current step executes that fallback while the cycle completes in the background, and the acquired rule serves later encounters. At 5 Hz the acquisition window spans about eight control cycles, during which the planner behaves as a verified conservative planner. Figure 10 contrasts the evaluated schedule with the deployment schedule.

D.9 Retrieval and Aggregation at Deployment Scale

As memory grows, retrieval and multi-rule aggregation must stay within the control window. The stress test runs on Highway and varies only the database size, inflating it with synthetic rules generated as variable and threshold perturbations of compiled rules that preserve the schema and the trigger-degree distribution (Table 20). Retrieval stays sub-millisecond and grows slowly with memory size, from 0.41 ms at the paper’s 1,023 rules to 0.79 ms at one hundred thousand, consistent with indexed lookup rather than linear scanning. Conflict aggregation does not grow with the database: retrieval returns at most k=10k{=}10 rules regardless of memory size, so noisy-OR aggregation (Eq. 5) and the arbitration of Appendix A.3 cost O⁡(k)O(k). On the online planning path, the database-size-dependent cost therefore concentrates in retrieval; index maintenance and write costs sit on the acquisition path, off the control loop.
